column4: Worldly life is likened to rain from the sky whose vegetation mingles with the earth and then becomes wind-scattered stubble, a complete growth-and-loss version of the section's field.
Water descends from the sky and the earth becomes green, directly condensing the section's ceiling-water and living-floor image.
The oath by the sky that returns rain names the repeatedly supplied water above the field whose opening is named in 86:12.
The oath by earth that cracks open gives a terse Quranic counterpart to the section's ploughed soil, opened watercourse, and emerging growth.
A garden of palms and grapes with rivers made to gush abundantly through it directly joins mature cultivation to the section's fajara water-opening.
Gardens, palms, and varied crops bear fruit and have a due given at harvest, connecting divinely produced growth to an ethical share of its yield.
The command to look at earth and the many noble pairs made to grow there directs the reader to the same divine husbandry as the section.
Earth is spread out and every beautiful pair is made to grow in it, explicitly combining the section's laid-out surface with fertility.
Earth is laid out for creatures, establishing the spread floor that the following two ayat fill with produce.
Fruit and palms with sheathed clusters occupy that laid-out earth, showing its mature yield.
Husked grain and fragrant plants complete the spread-earth sequence as a cultivated and provision-bearing surface.
The garden owner should have acknowledged Allah's will and that power belongs to Him; this states the divine dependence of the section's apparently human cultivation.
Believers are told to spend from the good things brought forth from earth and not select the bad, joining the spending parables' moral quality to the field's actual produce.
Allah will make earth's present adornment into barren dust, a direct terminus opposite the section's green, carpeted surface.
After the rain-and-revival sequence, a wind can leave the crop yellow and provoke ingratitude; it reverses the nurturing cloud into failed growth.
The wind sent against Aad is called barren, a wind that bears no nourishing rain and thus reverses the fertilizing winds and fertile ground of the section.
The barren wind leaves everything it reaches like decayed matter, giving the destructive yield of the sterile force named in 51:41.
Aad see a cloud approaching their valleys and expect rain, but it is the punishment they hastened; the apparent nurturing cloud carries the opposite outcome.
The wind destroys by its Lord's command until only dwellings remain visible, completing the reversal of hoped-for rain into a land emptied of life.
Some palms are cut down and others left standing on their roots, a Quranic boundary scene for the section's secondary sense of aqr as destroying a palm at its growing crown.
People are torn away like uprooted palm trunks, turning the section's plant-like human growth into the image of a people violently removed from their roots.
Aad lie like hollow, fallen palm trunks after the wind, another precise reversal of humans flourishing as plants.
The levelled earth becomes a smooth bare plain, an eschatological counterpart to the section's ground on which nothing can take root or grow.
The command to glorify the name of the Most High Lord introduces 87:2-5, where Rabb's creating, measuring, guiding, and bringing out pasture enact the section's nurture.
The Lord creates and proportions, supplying the ordered formation that precedes the pasture's growth and the soul's purification.
The Lord measures and guides, making gradual, directed development the bridge from creation to the pasture brought out in 87:4.
Allah makes earth a broad carpet for people, paralleling the section's spread floor and its low vegetation described as carpeting the surface.
Allah spreads earth and names Himself its excellent preparer, supporting the section's sense of a surface made fit to receive growth.
The command to look at how earth is spread makes the prepared horizontal surface itself an object of reflection, one component of the section's field-house.
The demanded sign is a spring made to gush from earth, isolating the same water-opening action that 17:91 places inside a garden.
The righteous make a spring gush abundantly, preserving the fajara branch's image of opening a controllable path for water in a different setting.
Allah brings living from dead and revives earth after its death, supporting the section's use of plant growth to make the living soul perceptible.
Earth splits away from people as they hasten out, turning the cracked-ground image into human emergence and extending the human-as-plant analogy to resurrection.
The garden's owner possesses abundant fruit and boasts of wealth, beginning the passage's exposure of a soul corrupted by gifted yield.
He enters his garden while wronging himself, explicitly placing the state of the nafs inside the cultivated landscape.
He assumes the garden will never perish and doubts the final return, mistaking contingent growth for permanent possession.
His companion recalls human creation from dust and then a drop, returning the proud cultivator himself to earthly, dependent beginnings.
The believing companion names Allah as his Lord and refuses partners, identifying the true Rabb behind the garden's nurture.
The garden owners make no exception to their harvest resolve, leaving their plan unqualified and setting up the exposure of assumed control over yield.
They urge one another to go early to their crop if they intend to harvest, keeping the destroyed garden explicitly within cultivated labour.
They plan that no poor person enter the garden, showing the moral barrenness accompanying their intended harvest.
On seeing the ruined garden they recognize themselves as deprived, naming the loss of yield their confidence had denied.
The most balanced among them recalls having urged glorification, shifting the failed field toward recognition of its Lord.
They glorify their Lord and confess wrongdoing, making repentance the first inner growth produced by the barren garden.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with a better one, reopening the possibility of growth under acknowledged divine nurture.
Humans are created from earth, returned into it, and brought out again; this distinguishes burial that leads to emergence from the section's smothering dassa.
The warning that the dismissive hearer may not purify himself clarifies the receptive boundary around the possible purification named in 80:3.
Clouds are driven, joined, and piled before rain emerges, detailing the cloud-to-rain process compressed into the section's extended meaning of sama.
Rain descends after people despair and divine mercy is spread, making water's arrival the reversal of an apparently hopeless dry condition.
Remaining upright is joined to being given abundant water, an indirect moral counterpart to the section's cultivated soul receiving ample irrigation.
The abundant water is itself a test, while turning from the Lord's reminder leads to severe punishment; provision therefore does not by itself prove inner fertility.
Spouses are described as tilth and the addressees are told to send ahead for themselves, extending field imagery from crop growth to human generation and moral consequence.
The measured rain and gardens of 23:18-19 continue in a tree from Sinai yielding oil and food, another mature product of divinely watered growth.
Allah causes a broad-leaved plant to grow over Jonah, a small human-and-plant scene in which divinely supplied growth shelters a recovering person.
A secure town receives abundant provision and then tastes hunger after ingratitude, translating the fertile field's moral dependence into communal provision and its withdrawal.
The question whether Thamud will be left secure amid what surrounds them introduces the gardens, springs, crops, and palms of 26:147-148 as vulnerable gifts.
